name: FastLanes
baseline: DuckDB (also compared against Apache Parquet+Snappy and Parquet+Zstd)
workload: Decoding/encoding throughput (rowgroups/sec) across real-world datasets and a single-value random-access latency micro-benchmark, comparing the FastLanes file format against DuckDB, Parquet+Snappy, Parquet+Zstd, and BtrBlocks.
claimed_speedup: On average 29x faster decoding/encoding throughput than DuckDB, 43x than Parquet+Snappy, 44x than Parquet+Zstd, 7x than BtrBlocks (Table 4); for single-value random access, 5x faster than DuckDB, 315x than Parquet+Snappy, 416x than Parquet+Zstd, 800x than BtrBlocks (Table 5)
compiler_and_flags: clang++; -O3, -O3 -mavx2, -O3 -mavx512dq for the SIMD micro-benchmarks (per Table in paper Sec. on micro-benchmarks)
hardware: Main throughput/decoding benchmark: AWS i4i.4xlarge, Intel Xeon Ice Lake, 16 vCPUs, 128GB RAM. The single-value random-access micro-benchmark (Table 5) was run separately on an Apple MacBook Pro M4 (different hardware, noted as a footnote in the paper).
tradeoffs: Encoding (compression) speed in the v0.1 code path is explicitly unoptimized per the paper; the file format only recently reached format-stability (v0.36+), so tooling/ecosystem support lags far behind Parquet; zero external dependencies but currently no true random-access-by-row-position support (block decode still required).
caveats: The headline multipliers are from the FastLanes authors' own VLDB 2025 paper ("The FastLanes File Format"), not an independent third party, though methodology, hardware, and compiler flags are fully documented and code is public, satisfying tier A. The random-access micro-benchmark used different hardware (Apple M4) than the main Ice Lake throughput benchmark, so those two numbers are not directly comparable to each other.
found_via: arXiv/DBLP search for cwida FastLanes VLDB papers; PDF opened directly at vldb.org/pvldb/vol18/p4629-afroozeh.pdf

name: ALP (Adaptive Lossless Floating-Point Compression)
baseline: Zstd, Gorilla, Chimp, Chimp128, Patas (existing lightweight and general-purpose floating-point compressors)
workload: Single/multi-threaded (1/8/16 thread) SCAN and SUM queries over compressed double/float columns from real-world datasets (food_prices, city_temperature, bitcoin_transactions, gov26, nyc29), plus separate compression-ratio benchmarks over the Public BI float/double corpus.
claimed_speedup: ALP is reported superior in decoding speed, compression ratio, and compression speed across every tested scheme (Gorilla, Chimp, Chimp128, Patas, Zstd, uncompressed, PDE) per the paper's results and the repo's benchmark CSVs; exact multipliers are in the repo's publication/end_to_end_bench results
compiler_and_flags: Clang++/g++ via CMake (>=3.22); exact build steps and flags documented in BENCHMARKING.md and run by publication/script/master_script.sh
hardware: Multiple documented target platforms in the reproducibility package: Intel Ice Lake (AVX512, e.g. AWS i4i.4xlarge), AMD Zen 3 (AVX2, AWS M6a/C6a), Apple M1, AWS Graviton 2/3 (NEON)
stars_or_usage: 234 stars; integrated into DuckDB, KuzuDB, and liquid-cache
tradeoffs: Targets IEEE754 float/double columns specifically, not general-purpose compression; decimal-heavy data benefits most, high-entropy/high-precision random values compress less well and fall back to a dictionary+FoR split scheme.
caveats: The SIGMOD 2024 paper itself is paywalled and has no arXiv preprint, so the exact headline multiplier was not read from the paper directly. Tier A is justified instead by the repo's ACM SIGMOD Availability & Reproducibility Initiative package (all three badges, including 'Results Reproduced'), which documents hardware, dependencies, and build/run steps end to end, and by the benchmark CSVs present in the repo.
found_via: Linked from the FastLanes README publications list; repo's availability_reproducibility_initiative_report.md

name: BtrBlocks
baseline: Apache Parquet (generated/read via the Apache Arrow C++ library) and Apache ORC
workload: In-memory decompression throughput and S3 cold-column-scan dollar-cost, measured on the 5 largest Public BI Benchmark datasets (~2451 columns) and all 22 TPC-H queries.
claimed_speedup: Decompresses 2.6x, 3.6x, 3.8x faster than uncompressed Parquet, Parquet+Snappy, and Parquet+Zstd respectively (average, Public BI Benchmark). Scanning individual columns from S3 is 9x cheaper than compressed Parquet variants and 20x cheaper than uncompressed Parquet on average; across all 22 TPC-H queries, Parquet/Parquet+Snappy/Parquet+Zstd cost 5.5x/3.6x/2.8x more than BtrBlocks.
hardware: AWS c5.metal / c5n.18xlarge: Intel Xeon Platinum 8000-series (Skylake-SP), 36x3.5GHz cores (72 threads), AVX2/AVX512, 100Gbps networking
tradeoffs: README states it 'currently requires an x86 platform' and is only built/tested on Linux and macOS; test suite described as 'rudimentary'; no true random-access-by-row API (would require reimplementation, per a later independent evaluation).
caveats: SIGMOD 2023 paper's own measurements (not independent), though hardware, compiler, and code are all public, satisfying tier A. A later, separate VLDB 2025 paper (FastLanes File Format, by an overlapping CWI research community) independently re-ran BtrBlocks on different hardware (AWS i4i.4xlarge) and found it 7x slower decoding/encoding than FastLanes, close to Parquet+Zstd's compression ratio, unable to benefit from AVX512, and could not be adapted for true single-value random access without a full API reimplementation -- weakening BtrBlocks' relative standing versus newer formats even though its original Parquet/ORC comparison holds up.
found_via: gh search repos 'btrblocks'; README's bit.ly/btrblocks link resolved to the TUM-hosted SIGMOD 2023 PDF

name: Vortex
workload: First-party benchmark suite (bench.vortex.dev) covering write throughput, full-table scan throughput, hot/cold single-row random-access latency, a ClickBench run using DataFusion as the query engine, and a TPC-H SF=1 NVMe run, all vs. Apache Parquet.
claimed_speedup: 2.97x write throughput; 30.73x scan throughput (84.14 GB/s); hot random access 1.15x at 1.85ms vs. Parquet's cold read of 65.32s (~627x, mixed cold/hot comparison); ClickBench-with-DataFusion 1.13x (3.99s vs 6.08s); TPC-H SF1/NVMe 1.32x (450.40ms)
stars_or_usage: 3.2k stars; Linux Foundation LF AI & Data incubation project
tradeoffs: Rust-native (needs FFI/bindings for direct C++ use, though it advertises zero-copy Arrow compatibility); file format only reached 'stable' status from v0.36.0 onward; young ecosystem versus Parquet's universal tooling support.
caveats: bench.vortex.dev does not state a CPU/hardware model or compiler flags on the page itself (only links out to GitHub for 'detailed description'), so this falls short of tier A/B despite the benchmark code being public. More importantly, when the query ENGINE is held constant (DuckDB), ClickHouse/ClickBench's own public results for duckdb-vortex vs duckdb-parquet (2026-05-11 run, c6a.4xlarge) show Vortex was actually SLOWER on the standard ClickBench workload: 40.99s vs 32.48s total (sum of best-of-3 across the 43 queries; derived from page data in ClickHouse/ClickBench's results JSON files), and a later 'tuned' duckdb-vortex run had a much higher load time (762s). This directly contradicts the vendor's 'faster scans' headline for the DuckDB-with-Vortex integration path, even though Vortex's own DataFusion-based ClickBench comparison on bench.vortex.dev shows a (smaller) win.
found_via: gh api repos/vortex-data/vortex; WebFetch of bench.vortex.dev; ClickHouse/ClickBench GitHub repo (duckdb-vortex and duckdb-parquet results/20260511/c6a.4xlarge.json)

name: Lance
workload: Random-access point lookups and full-scan throughput on NVMe-backed storage, per the VLDB 2025 paper 'Lance: Efficient Random Access in Columnar Storage through Adaptive Structural Encodings' (hardware: NVMe drive + Intel i7-10700K, 8 cores/16 threads).
claimed_speedup: README/homepage marketing claim: '100x faster random access than Parquet or Iceberg'. The peer-reviewed VLDB 2025 paper is more nuanced: its own abstract states 'Parquet, when configured correctly, can achieve over 60x better random access performance than default settings' -- i.e. most of the headline 100x gap is against Parquet's poorly-tuned defaults, not a well-tuned Parquet baseline; Lance's actual claimed contribution is matching/exceeding well-tuned Parquet's random access without giving up scan throughput or RAM usage.
hardware: NVMe drive with an Intel i7-10700K CPU (8 cores/16 threads), per the VLDB 2025 paper
tradeoffs: Rust-native with Python/Java bindings (pylance); optimized for AI/ML lakehouse workloads (multimodal blobs, vector indexes, data versioning) rather than general OLAP scans; file format still evolving under a data_storage_version compatibility contract.
caveats: The widely repeated '100x faster than Parquet' figure is a marketing headline (README/homepage), not a number found stated verbatim in the peer-reviewed paper; the paper itself undercuts the headline by showing well-tuned Parquet already recovers most (60x) of that gap versus default Parquet settings, so this is downgraded from the vendor's implied claim to tier C pending a clean apples-to-apples number against tuned Parquet.
found_via: gh api repos/lance-format/lance; WebFetch lance.org homepage; arXiv abstract 2504.15247

name: StarRocks
workload: Star Schema Benchmark (SSB), 13 queries on flat tables (vendor blog post dated Aug 21, 2023)
claimed_speedup: "ClickHouse has a response time 2.2x slower than that of StarRocks" on SSB (vendor blog; hardware/compiler not stated in the post)
tradeoffs: MPP architecture with a separate Java frontend (FE, planner/metadata) and C++ backend (BE, vectorized execution engine) -- heavier operational footprint than embedded engines like DuckDB; MySQL-wire compatible.
caveats: The 2.2x claim is from StarRocks' own 2023 blog post with no hardware/CPU model or compiler flags stated (tier C). It is directly CONTRADICTED by ClickHouse's own independent, reproducible ClickBench suite: on identical c6a.4xlarge hardware, ClickHouse's 2026-09-26 run totals 18.03s (sum of best-of-3 across the 43 ClickBench queries) versus StarRocks' 2026-09-07 run at 44.47s -- i.e. ClickHouse is now roughly 2.5x FASTER than StarRocks on ClickBench, the reverse of the vendor's SSB claim (derived from page data: ClickHouse/ClickBench GitHub repo, clickhouse/results/20260926/c6a.4xlarge.json vs starrocks/results/20260907/c6a.4xlarge.json). The discrepancy likely reflects ~3 years of ClickHouse improvements plus workload differences (SSB star-schema joins vs. ClickBench's flat-table scans), but it substantially weakens confidence in the vendor claim as a current, general statement.
found_via: gh api repos/StarRocks/starrocks/contents/README.md; WebFetch starrocks.io/blog/benchmark-test; ClickHouse/ClickBench GitHub repo

name: Crystal (GPU query-processing library)
baseline: MonetDB (and Hyper, a commercial closed-source DBMS, reported for reference)
workload: 13 Star Schema Benchmark queries, comparing a CPU-vectorized implementation (Intel i7-6900K, Skylake, 8 cores, AVX2) against a GPU implementation using the Crystal CUDA device-function library (Nvidia Tesla V100, CUDA 10.0), Ubuntu 16.04.
claimed_speedup: Crystal-on-GPU is on average 2.5x faster than MonetDB-on-CPU and 1.17x faster than Hyper-on-CPU across the SSB queries; some individual queries show >5x speedups over both
compiler_and_flags: CUDA 10.0 (nvcc) for the GPU build; exact optimization flags for the CPU/GPU builds are not stated in the paper
hardware: CPU: single-socket Intel i7-6900K (Skylake, 8 cores, AVX2 256-bit SIMD); GPU: Nvidia Tesla V100 (measured bidirectional PCIe bandwidth 12.8 GB/s); Ubuntu 16.04
tradeoffs: Requires an Nvidia GPU and CUDA toolchain; provides block-wide device-function building blocks and SSB query implementations rather than a full SQL engine; the paper's own cost analysis weighs the ~$3/hr V100 rental cost against the speedup rather than declaring an unconditional win.
caveats: Published SIGMOD 2020, predating DuckDB/ClickHouse/Arrow-based baselines, so its named baselines (MonetDB, Hyper) are not in the assignment's baseline list; recorded honestly with baseline_in_list=false since MonetDB is a widely used, historically foundational column-store incumbent. Compiler optimization flags are not stated in the paper, which caps the tier at B rather than A. Last commit 2024; effectively an academic reference implementation rather than an actively maintained library today.
found_via: gh search repos 'crystal' 'GPU' 'query'; paper PDF at anilshanbhag.in/static/papers/crystal_sigmod20.pdf
